title: Test Your Understanding: CDN and Edge Caching
description: Static vs dynamic, TTL, invalidation, origin shield, and cache-key failure modes — not just definitions.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of putting a CDN in front of your origin for static assets?

options.text: It makes database queries faster
It serves cached copies from edge locations near users, reducing latency and origin load
It automatically makes all API responses globally consistent
It replaces the need for application caches like Redis

questions.explanation: CDNs cache cacheable responses at PoPs close to users. Hits avoid the long round trip to origin and spare origin bandwidth. They don't fix uncacheable APIs or replace app-level caches for personalized data.

questions.question: Which response is safest to cache at a shared CDN edge with a long TTL?

options.text: `/api/me` returning the logged-in user's profile
`/app.a1b2c3.js` with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`
HTML page with server-rendered user name in the navbar
API response with `Set-Cookie` and `Cache-Control: public`

questions.explanation: Hashed, versioned static assets are content-addressable — URL changes when content changes, so long TTLs are safe. Personalized or cookie-bound responses must not live in a shared edge cache without explicit, reviewed key rules.

questions.question: On a CDN cache miss, what happens?

options.text: The request fails; CDNs never contact the origin
The edge fetches from origin, may store the response, and returns it to the user
The edge always redirects the user to the origin URL
The edge waits until TTL expires before fetching

questions.explanation: Miss path: edge → origin → edge caches (if cacheable) → user. First request to a PoP after purge or cold start pays origin latency; that's why warm-up and smart invalidation matter.

questions.question: What is the best invalidation strategy for fingerprinted JS/CSS bundles from a frontend build?

options.text: Purge `/*` on every deploy
Version the URL (hash in filename) and use a long TTL — no purge needed for old files
Set TTL to zero permanently
Disable CDN caching for all JavaScript

questions.explanation: Content-hashed filenames make each deploy a new URL. Old caches naturally become irrelevant; new files get cached with aggressive TTL. Purging everything causes origin refill storms.

questions.question: What does `stale-while-revalidate` in `Cache-Control` enable?

options.text: Serving stale content forever without revalidation
Serving slightly stale content quickly while fetching a fresh copy in the background
Bypassing the CDN entirely
Encrypting cached responses at the edge

questions.explanation: After max-age expires, stale-while-revalidate lets the edge return stale bytes immediately while revalidating asynchronously — better UX than blocking on origin during refresh.

questions.question: Why use origin shield (tiered caching)?

options.text: To eliminate the need for cache headers
To collapse many edge-to-origin fetches into fewer shield-to-origin fetches when PoPs miss
To store user session data at the edge
To replace DNS

questions.explanation: When many regional edges miss at once (after purge or launch), shield sits between edges and origin — one fill can serve many edges, protecting a fragile or expensive origin from thundering herds.

questions.question: You cached an API response at the CDN without including `Authorization` in the cache key. What is the likely failure?

options.text: Higher database CPU only
One user's response may be served to another user — a cache key / data leak bug
Automatic purge of all cookies
TLS certificate errors

questions.explanation: Shared caches key on URL (and configured headers). If the body varies by user but the key doesn't, the first response wins for everyone. Authenticated APIs should use `private, no-store` or separate hostnames — not shared CDN caching.

questions.question: Setting `Cache-Control: public` on a response that includes a session cookie is a safe way to cache it at the CDN edge.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Cookies do not automatically prevent CDN storage. `public` allows shared caches to store the response. Session-specific bodies need `private, no-store` or strict cache-key design — default to not caching authenticated responses at the edge.
